core: Active listening as a trainable, observable, assessable behavior set rather than a disposition

Origin and attribution: Rogers and Farson's 1957 Industrial Relations Center pamphlet; Thomas Gordon's account that he developed the reflecting technique at the University of Chicago Counseling Center in 1946-47 and adopted the name at Farson's suggestion
Attending and nonverbal presence, with the honest caveat that nonverbal norms vary across cultures and individuals so rules like 'maintain eye contact' fail as universals
The micro-skills: minimal encouragers / back-channel cues, paraphrase, reflection of feeling, summarizing, and open versus closed questions
The distinction between a reflection (statement form, listener carries the risk) and a question (interrogative form, speaker carries the burden of answering)
Gordon's twelve communication roadblocks, why premature reassurance closes a topic, and the sequencing point that advice is not banned but is wrong when it arrives before understanding
Silence as a deliberate tool, and clarifying and checking understanding rather than assuming
Listening for content, feeling, and meaning as three separable layers
Documenting accurately afterward, and distinguishing quotation from paraphrase from inference in the record
Listening in interpreter-mediated encounters under the NCIHC national standards of practice
Listening on the phone and on video, where visual back-channel cues are degraded or absent
Honest evidence appraisal: the listening bundle has experimental support; individual micro-skills have thinner and mixed support
supporting: The five-stage listening process (receiving, interpreting, recalling, evaluating, responding) and the hearing/listening distinction
The speech-rate versus thought-rate gap as a mechanism for attention drift
National CLAS Standards 5-8 on language assistance, interpreter competence, and avoiding untrained individuals and minors as interpreters
Cochrane evidence on what communication skills training does and does not change

OARS as a motivational interviewing structure, MI spirit, change talk, and sustain talk - owned by the motivational-interviewing-basics topic

claims.claim: The phrase 'active listening' was popularized by a short 1957 work by Carl R. Rogers and Richard E. Farson, published by the University of Chicago Industrial Relations Center and later reissued as a 40-page book, which applied counseling methods to workplace conversation and argued that a listener must attend to emotional undertones as well as verbal content.

By the account of the organization Thomas Gordon founded, Gordon developed the practice of reflecting clients' meanings and feelings while working at the University of Chicago Counseling Center in 1946-47, and later adopted the label 'Active Listening' after his former student Richard Farson suggested it.

Gordon's twelve communication roadblocks grew out of his doctoral dissertation research, building on studies by Carl Rogers' students of therapist responses that blocked client communication, and became the twelve roadblocks taught in his first leadership training program in 1957; Parent Effectiveness Training was published in 1970.

Gordon's roadblock list is conventionally given as twelve responses, commonly named as ordering/directing, warning/threatening, moralizing/preaching, advising or giving solutions, persuading with logic or arguing, judging/criticizing/blaming, praising or agreeing, name-calling or ridiculing, analyzing or diagnosing, reassuring or sympathizing, probing and questioning, and diverting/sarcasm/withdrawal; the exact wording varies between Gordon Training International's own renderings, one of which substitutes teaching/lecturing and sarcasm/humor.

Gordon Training International describes roadblocks as responses that stop the other person talking, take responsibility for solving the problem away from them, and communicate non-acceptance of the person as they are, and it calls the set the 'Dirty Dozen'.

Listening is standardly modelled as a multi-stage process - receiving, interpreting, recalling, evaluating, and responding - that is distinct from hearing, and receiving draws on both auditory and visual channels.

Back-channel cues include verbal signals such as 'uh-huh', 'oh', and 'right' and nonverbal signals such as direct eye contact, head nods, and leaning forward; delivering them on autopilot produces pseudo-listening, which listeners are generally detected doing.
People speak at roughly 125 to 175 words per minute while listeners can process between 400 and 800 words per minute, and this gap is a standard explanation for attention drift during listening.

Listening expectations vary by cultural context: high-context settings place more weight on silence and nonverbal cues while low-context settings rely on explicit verbal statement, and looking away from a speaker can indicate cognitive processing rather than inattention, so fixed nonverbal rules such as 'maintain eye contact' are unreliable as universals.

In a 2010 experiment with 180 undergraduates, participants who received a paraphrased reflection rather than a simple acknowledgement rated the listener as more socially attractive, but paraphrasing was not associated with greater conversational satisfaction or with feeling more understood.

A 2020 Journal of Experimental Social Psychology paper defined high-quality listening as conveying empathy, interest-taking, and unconditional regard, and across a pilot plus three studies (N = 952) reported that high-quality listening predicted greater speaker self-insight (d = 1.19), greater openness to attitude change (d = 0.46), and lower prejudiced attitudes (d = 0.32), with self-insight mediating the effects.

The authors of that listening study noted limits: participants may have chosen moderate rather than extreme prejudices, the comparisons were short-term rather than baseline attitude change, the outcomes were self-reported and vulnerable to social desirability, and long-term effects were not examined.

The 2018 Cochrane review of communication skills training for healthcare professionals working with people who have cancer included 17 randomized trials with 1,240 professionals and found that trained professionals were more likely to use open questions and to show empathy and less likely to give facts only, with moderate- to low-certainty evidence.

The same Cochrane review found no significant differences for eliciting patient concerns, providing appropriate information, clarifying and summarizing, or negotiation skills, no evidence of benefit for professional burnout or for patients' satisfaction, perceptions of communication, or mental or physical health (very low-certainty evidence), and could not determine whether training effects are sustained over time or which programs work best.

The NCIHC National Standards of Practice for Interpreters in Health Care (2005) direct the interpreter to render all messages accurately and completely without adding, omitting, or substituting; to replicate the register, style, and tone of the speaker; to advise parties that everything said will be interpreted; to manage the flow of communication, for example by asking a speaker to pause or slow down; to correct errors in interpretation; and to maintain transparency about any side exchange.

The same standards direct the interpreter to promote direct communication among all parties - for example by telling the patient and provider to address each other rather than the interpreter - and to limit professional activity to interpreting within the encounter, so that an interpreter never advises a patient on health care questions but redirects the question to the provider.

The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Office of Minority Health National CLAS Standards require organizations to offer language assistance to people with limited English proficiency at no cost to them, to inform people that it is available, and to ensure the competence of those providing it, stating that the use of untrained individuals and minors as interpreters should be avoided and discouraged.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Does paraphrasing, on its own, make speakers feel understood?
positions: Practice texts and training curricula present paraphrase as the mechanism by which a speaker feels heard.

Weger, Castle, and Emmett (2010) found paraphrase raised ratings of the listener's social attractiveness but did not raise conversational satisfaction or felt understanding relative to a simple acknowledgement.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches paraphrase as a craft skill while stating plainly that the isolated experimental effect is narrower than training materials imply, and that the better-supported finding concerns listening quality as a bundle (empathy, interest, unconditional regard) rather than any single move.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Does communication skills training improve outcomes for the people served?
positions: Training programs are widely mandated on the assumption that better listening improves client experience and wellbeing.

The 2018 Cochrane review found trained behaviors changed (more open questions, more empathy) but reported no evidence of benefit for patient satisfaction, perceptions of communication, or health, and no effect on professional burnout, at very low certainty.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states both findings and distinguishes 'the behavior can be trained' from 'the trained behavior demonstrably improves downstream outcomes', which is the honest position given current evidence.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Do fixed nonverbal rules such as 'maintain eye contact' constitute good practice guidance?
positions: Many introductory checklists teach attending as a fixed posture, including sustained eye contact.
Listening norms differ between high-context and low-context settings, and looking away can signal cognitive processing rather than inattention.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches attending as adjustable behavior to be calibrated and checked with the person, and explicitly rejects universal nonverbal rules.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Exact membership of Gordon's twelve roadblocks.
positions: One Gordon Training International page lists persuading with logic/arguing and diverting/sarcasm/withdrawal.
Another Gordon Training International page lists teaching/lecturing and sarcasm/humor instead.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson names the twelve in their most common form and states that the phrasing varies across Gordon's own publications, rather than presenting one list as canonical.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft contained no substantive claims about listening at all; its body text was subject-agnostic filler that would apply to any topic in any subject.

The draft's analogy (a label on a toolbox drawer) and its worked example (a student reading a scenario) described study technique rather than a practice skill, and were unsupported by anything about listening.
The draft's three quick-check items tested generic study advice about definitions and context, not any listening content, and each offered only three options.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the entire lesson body with sourced content on the micro-skills, Gordon's roadblocks, and the evidence base.
Added the attribution history the draft omitted: Rogers and Farson 1957, and Gordon's own account of developing the technique and adopting Farson's label.
Replaced the abstract worked example with a transcript-style craft example that diagnoses three weak practitioner responses and rewrites each.
Added the honest evidence statement the draft lacked, including the Cochrane finding of no demonstrated downstream benefit and the Weger paraphrasing null results.
Added interpreter-mediated and remote-contact practice, which the draft did not mention.
Rejected universal nonverbal rules in favor of calibrated attending, since the sources support variation by culture and individual.
rightsIssues: Gordon Training International pages carry an explicit all-rights-reserved copyright notice. Used as REFERENCE_ONLY: the roadblock categories are named and described in original wording, and no page text is reproduced.

The LibreTexts adaptation of Communication in the Real World is CC BY-NC-SA 3.0. Because the non-commercial condition may conflict with this project's use, the source was treated as REFERENCE_ONLY and no wording was adapted from it.
The Cochrane review and the Journal of Experimental Social Psychology article are commercially published and rights-restricted; findings are reported as facts in original wording, with no excerpting.
The NCIHC National Standards of Practice is a standards-body publication with no explicit open license located; treated as REFERENCE_ONLY and described rather than quoted.
The HHS Office of Minority Health CLAS Standards are published by a U.S. federal agency, but reuse rights were not separately verified on the page, so the source is recorded as REFERENCE_ONLY.
Rogers and Farson's 1957 text is in copyright and was not accessed in full; it is cited from a bibliographic record for attribution only, and no claims are made about its wording.

sourceRecords.title: Active Listening (bibliographic record)
sourceRecords.notes: Used only to verify the attribution and publication facts for Rogers and Farson's Active Listening: authors, original 1957 publication, later 40-page reissue by Mockingbird Press (2021), and the work's stated focus on applying counseling method to workplace conversation. No text from the work itself is used.

sourceRecords.title: Origins of the Gordon Model
sourceRecords.license: All rights reserved (© Gordon Training International)
sourceRecords.notes: Supports the historical account: Gordon developed empathic reflecting at the University of Chicago Counseling Center in 1946-47; Richard Farson suggested the term 'Active Listening'; the roadblocks came from Gordon's dissertation research building on Rogers' students' work and became twelve roadblocks in his 1957 leadership program; P.E.T. published 1970. Described in original wording; no page text reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: What Are the Roadblocks to Helping Your Child?
sourceRecords.license: All rights reserved (© Gordon Training International)
sourceRecords.notes: Supports the canonical twelve-item roadblock list and its stated effects (the other person stops talking, loses ownership of the problem, hears non-acceptance). Categories are named and explained in original wording.

sourceRecords.title: Do You Use the Dirty Dozen When You Communicate?
sourceRecords.license: All rights reserved (© Gordon Training International)
sourceRecords.notes: Supports the 'Dirty Dozen' nickname and an alternative rendering of the list (including teaching/lecturing and sarcasm/humor), which is the evidence for the lesson's statement that the exact wording varies across Gordon's publications.

sourceRecords.title: Communication in the Real World: An Introduction to Communication Studies, Chapter 5 — Listening
sourceRecords.notes: Supports the hearing/listening distinction, the five-stage listening process, back-channel cues, pseudo-listening, the speech-rate versus thought-rate gap, the point that looking away may reflect processing rather than inattention, and high-context versus low-context differences in the weight given to silence and nonverbal cues. Treated as reference only because of the non-commercial license condition; no wording adapted.

sourceRecords.title: Active Listening in Peer Interviews: The Influence of Message Paraphrasing on Perceptions of Listening Skill
sourceRecords.notes: Weger, Castle, and Emmett (2010), 180 undergraduates, paraphrase versus simple acknowledgement in peer interviews. Supports the finding that paraphrase was associated with the listener's social attractiveness but not with conversational satisfaction or feeling understood — the lesson's central caution about component-level evidence.

sourceRecords.title: Can high quality listening predict lower speakers' prejudiced attitudes?
sourceRecords.provider: Journal of Experimental Social Psychology (via PubMed Central)
sourceRecords.notes: Itzchakov, Weinstein, Legate, and Amar (2020), DOI 10.1016/j.jesp.2020.104022. Supports the operational definition of high-quality listening (empathy, interest-taking, unconditional regard), the reported effects on self-insight, openness to attitude change, and prejudiced attitudes, and the authors' own stated limitations.

sourceRecords.title: Communication skills training for healthcare professionals working with people who have cancer (Cochrane review, 2018 update)
sourceRecords.provider: Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews (via PubMed Central)
sourceRecords.notes: Moore, Rivera, Bravo-Soto, Olivares, and Lawrie (2018). Supports the trained-behavior findings (more open questions, more empathy, fewer facts-only responses), the null findings (eliciting concerns, appropriate information, clarifying and summarizing, negotiation; burnout; patient satisfaction, perception, and health), and the certainty and durability caveats.

sourceRecords.title: National Standards of Practice for Interpreters in Health Care
sourceRecords.provider: National Council on Interpreting in Health Care
sourceRecords.notes: September 2005; 32 standards under nine headings. Supports the accuracy standards (render all messages completely without adding, omitting, or substituting; replicate register, style, and tone; advise parties that everything will be interpreted; manage flow; correct errors; maintain transparency), the respect standards (promote direct communication among parties), and the role-boundary standards (limit professional activity to interpreting; never advise, but redirect).

sourceRecords.title: National Standards for Culturally and Linguistically Appropriate Services (CLAS) in Health and Health Care
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Office of Minority Health (Think Cultural Health)
sourceRecords.notes: Supports Standards 5-8: language assistance offered at no cost to the individual, notice that it is available, verification of the competence of those providing it with untrained individuals and minors avoided and discouraged as interpreters, and easy-to-understand materials and signage. Rights not separately verified on the page, so treated as reference only.
